The mystery cult of Kabeiros and his attendant Child (Pais) in Boeotia was connected with young men, who were subjected to trials in order to ensure fertility and strength, the main qualities of a man.

title: Bronze statue of Poseidon. From the sea area east of the bay of Livadostra in Boeotia, where ancient Kreusis is located, the port of Plataia. About 480 BC (X 11761).
description: The god is depicted nude, with his right foot advanced, standing on a bronze base with the inscription ΤΟ ΠΟΤΕΙΔΑΟΝΟΣ ΗΙΑΡΟΣ (“Sacred to Poseidon”). In the left raised hand he will have hold the trident, while on the right possibly a dolphin. The eyes were made of a different material and inlaid. The lips are rendered with reddish copper. The work is one of the few original works dating at the beginning of the Severe Style.

title: Bronze statue of Poseidon or Zeus. From the sea area near Cape Artemision, Northern Euboea. About 460 BC (X 15161).
description: The god is shown in wide stride, extending the left arm forward, while with the right he will have hold a trident or a thunderbolt. Opinions differ as to whether Poseidon or Zeus is depictted. The statue is one of the few surviving original works of the Sever Style with magnificent rendering of the movement and the formation of the body, undoubtedly the creation of a great sculptor of the Early Classical period.

title: Bronze figurine of Zeus Ceraunaeus. From the Sanctuary of Zeus at Dodona. 470-460 BC (Χ 16546).
description: The type of the god in a striding stance, extending the left arm forward and holding the thunderbolt in his right hand is known from other figurines, as well as from vase painting and coins. The thunderbolt is a symbol of the presence and authority of the omnipotent god, who seeks to impose the divine order in the world.

title: Bronze figurine of a seated goddess. From the sanctuary of Demeter and Kore at Ayios Sostis in Arcadia. A work in the tradition of northeastern Peloponnese, and especially Argos. About 470 BC (X 14922).
description: The stance of the seated, frontal figure and the fruit (pomegranate and possibly apple) in her hands identify her with Demeter, patron goddess of agriculture.

title: Βronze statuette of a peplos-clad maiden. From the region of Mount Pindos, Northwestern Greece. 460-450 BC (Καρ. 540).
description: The figure wears a long Doric dress (peplos) over a pleated chiton and was probably holding a flower in her right hand. This symbol, combined with the pigeon in her left hand, leads to the identification of the figure with the goddess Aphrodite.

title: Bronze stand-mirror supported by the figure of peplos-clad maiden standing on a tripod base. Unknown provenance. Argive workshop. About 455 BC (X 7579).
description: The opposed pairs of figures around the border of the disc - cupids, hounds, hares, cocks - are associated with the women’s world. Mirrors of this type were luxury objects due to their rarity and workmanship.

title: Bronze statuette of an athlete. From Sikyona (Peloponnese). About 440 BC (X 7474).
description: The youth turns his head to the left, maybe looking at an object (bowl?) in his hand. It is most probably modelled on a large work created in the artistic circle of the renowned sculptor Polykleitos.

title: Bronze Hermes figurine. From the Sanctuary of Zeus on Mount Lykaion in Arcadia. 5th cent. BC (Χ 13219).
description: The god is represented in shepherd's clothing: a short tunic, a chlamys and a conical cap (pilos). From the characteristic Hermes’s

title: Cheekpiece of a bronze helmet. From the sanctuary of Zeus at Dodona. About 400 BC (Καρ. 166)
description: It bears a relief scene showing a battle between two warriors, maybe Polydeuces, son of Zeus (Dioskouros), against his cousin Lynceus.

title: Bronze statue of a young athlete found in the sea off Marathon, Attica. Around 340-330 BC (X 15118).
description: The statue probably depicts the young winner of a contest, as is suggested by the band on his head which ends in an upright leaf above the forehead. The object he held in his raised right hand is not preserved. It is also unclear what he held in his left hand, toward which he turns his head and gazes steadily. The inlaid eyes were made of white stone with yellowish glass paste for the irises. The harmonic proportions of the body, the mild fluid musculature, the smooth transitions from one surface to the other, the almost transverse posture of the body and the free but peaceful movement of the figure in space connect the work with the Praxiteles School and place it between the masterpieces of the Late Classical period.

title: Bronze statue of a youth. From the Antikythera shipwreck (retrieved in 1900-1901). Around 340-330 BC (X 13396).
description: The figure is identified either with Perseus holding the head of Medusa in his right hand or more possibly with Paris holding the Apple of Discord to give it to the most beautiful of the goddesses, Aphrodite. The tradition of Polykleitos is evident in the whole structure of the figure and the intense musculature. The attribution of the statue to a specific artist finds the scholars divided. An artist from the circle of the Parian sculptor Skopas, or the Corinthian sculptor Euphranor are among the candidates. At any rate, the majority of scholars, in considering the “Antikythera Youth” as a work of the Argive-Sicyonian school of successors to Polykleitos, are inclined to attribute it to the Sicyonian Kleon.

title: Bronze portrait head of a boxer. From the sanctuary of Zeus at Olympia. Around 330-320 BC (X 6439).
description: The head is crowned with “kotinos”, the olive-branch wreath awarded to victors in the Olympic Games, of which only the stem is preserved. The individual facial features have led to the identification of the figure as a boxer. The head probably belonged to a statue of the famous boxer Satyros of Elis, who repeatedly won in the boxing event at Nemea, Pythia and Olympia. The statue of the boxer Satyros at Olympia was the work of the Athenian bronze-sculptor Silanion.

title: Bronze urn hydria. From Pharsala, Thessaly. Around 370 BC (Χ 18775).
description: The lower attachment of the vertical handle is decorated with the relief mythical scene of the abduction of the Athenian princess Oreithyia by Boreas, king of Thrace. The vase contained the cremated bones of Asterios, whose name was incised on a gold plate found inside it.

title: Bronze figurine of a general and liver diviner. From the sanctuary of Zeus at Dodona. About 300 BC (Χ 16727).
description: He holds the liver of a sacrificed animal for divination purposes.  Although fortune-telling by means of liver after a sacrifice was a usual practice in antiquity, in order to foresee the outcome of a coming confrontation, the relevant representations are rare. The statuette imitates in miniature scale monumental statues of generals of the Epirote League, fragments of which have been found in the sanctuary of Dodona. It is probably depicted Kineas, philosopher and adviser to Pyrrhus, king of Epirus.

title: Portrait head and parts of a bronze statue of a philosopher. From the Antikythera Shipwreck (retrieved in 1900–1901). Ca. 230 BC or shortly thereafter (Χ 13400, X 15105, X 15108, X 15091, X 15090, X 18932, X 15088).
description: In addition to the head, two parts of the himation are preserved along with both legs from about the middle of the shins, the right arm and the left hand. The philosopher was depicted standing, wearing a long himation that covered the larger part of his body and was folded back on his left shoulder. He held a staff in his left hand and his right arm was bent at the elbow, his hand extended in a gesture characteristic of people delivering a speech. On his feet he wore thick-soled sandals of the trochades type with crossed straps, tied above the ankles. The portrait depicts a Cynic philosopher, probably Bion the Borysthenite.

title: Bronze statuette of Dionysos. From Chochlia, Evrytania. About mid-2nd cent. BC (X 15209).
description: The god is represented as a beautiful youth with his attributes. He wears an ivy wreath on the head, a short light tunic (chiton), a fawnskin and boots. He will have hold a wand wreathed in ivy-and vine-leaves with a pine cone at the top (thyrsus) in the right hand and a drinking cup (kantharos) in the left. The naturalistic work is influenced by the works of monumental sculpture.

title: Bronze statue of a horse and a young jockey. Found in the sea off Cape Artemision, North Euboea.  About 140 BC (X 15177).
description: Retrieved in 1928 and 1937 in pieces from the seafloor off Cape Artemision, north Euboea. The young jockey, probably African in origin, will have held the reins of the galloping horse in his left hand and a whip in his right. The contractions and furrows in his face, especially on the forehead, reveal agony and passion. The work is known as the Artemision Jockey.

title: Bronze portrait head. From Delos (Palaestra of Granite). End of 2nd - beginning of 1st cent. BC (X 14612).
description: Fleshy, discreetly realistic male portrait. Wrinkles on the forehead and at the edges of the eyes, melancholic expression with a wet look, which becomes more vivid thanks to the multicolor of the eyes, are characteristics that contradict the idealism of the classic rule.

title: The Antikythera Mechanism. From the Antikythera Shipwreck. 2nd half of the 2nd cent. BC (X 15087).
description: Seven large fragments (Α-G) and 75 minor pieces (1-75) have survived. Their exact position and the original structure of the Mechanism are still a matter of intense investigation. It contained at least 30 gearwheels as well as dials, scales, axles and pointers. The greek, astronomical inscriptions on the surface of the Mechanism refer to astronomical and calendar calculations, while the inscriptions on its metal protective plates contain instructions for its use. The Mechanism was protected by a wooden case, which had a bronze plaque on the front and another one at the back side. The Antikythera Mechanism is the earliest preserved portable astronomical calculator. It displayed the positions of the Sun, the Moon and most probably the five planets known in antiquity, Mercury, Venus, Mars, Jupiter and Saturn. It was used to predict solar and lunar eclipses, it kept an accurate calendar of many years and displayed the date of the Panhellenic games held at Olympia, Delphi, Nemea, Isthmia   and Dodona.

title: Βronze inscribed plaque. From the Sanctuary of Zeus at Olympia. 300-250 BC (Χ 6442).
description: The plaque contains an honorary decree passed by the Eleians for the wrestler Demokrates, who won in the men’s wrestling at the Olympic Games. The athlete was proclaimed benefactor and was granted exemption from tax, the right to own land in the region of Elis and to participate in festivals and sacrifices. The decree was to be inscribed on a bronze plaque, set up in the sanctuary of Zeus at Olympia and sent to the Tenedians, Demokrates’ fellows. In the triangular pediment are depicted the symbols of the island of Tenedos and the god Dionysos, a bunch of grapes and two double axes. By means of such a tool the Tenedians used to slaughter a young calf at their festivals in honour of Dionysos, from which everyone had to eat in order to ingest the god himself. Pausanias (6.17.1) mentions that in the sanctuary of Olympia there was a statue of Demokrates.

title: Bronze statue of the emperor Augustus (27 BC - AD 14), found in the Aegean Sea between the islands of Euboea and Agios Efstratios. 12-10 BC (X 23322).
description: The emperor is depicted in mature age, mounting a horse. He wears a tunica with a vertical purple stripe (clavus purpurea) and a fringed paludamentum decorated with a maeander pattern. Iconographic features of the Prima Porta and Actium types are combined in this statue. The right hand is raised in a gesture of official greeting. The hilt of his sword can be seen below the left hand, in which he held the horse’s reigns. On the bezel of his finger-ring a staff of divination (lituus) is engraved, symbolising the supreme religious office of Pontifex Maximus, assumed by Augustus in 12 BC.

title: Bronze portrait statue of the empress Julia Aquilia Severa. From Sparta, Lakonia.  AD 221-222 (X 23321).
description: The woman wears a chiton and a himation and will have had a crown on her head. The coiffure which is characteristic of the Severan dynasty, combined with the extensive damage attributed to damnatio memoriae (posthumous condemnation involving the destruction of images and the erasing of the name of the condemned person from public monuments), had led to the identification of the figure depicted with one of the leading female figures of the Severan dynasty who suffered this fate. Julia Aquilia was the second and then the fourth and last wife of the emperor Heliogabalus (AD 218-222). There is no evidence that Julia Aquilia Severa suffered damnatio memoriae. The poor condition of the statue is the result of the collapse of the building in which it was erected, caused by a fire, as it is clear from the excavation record.

The Egyptians believed that the boat would carry them, even after death, to Abydos, to participate in the sacred pilgrimage of Osiris. They also believed that the sun god Re himself was travelling across the sky each morning and to the Underworld during night in his divine barque. Ships were made of papyrus or wood. Helped by Nile currents and the north wind, they travelled downriver with oars and upriver with sails.

description: Priests, whose office was usually hereditary, were a particularly privileged class in Egyptian society. The pharaoh was the high priest, who ceded his ritual duties to the order of high priests. Priests were divided into categories according to their duties (treasurer, astronomer, lector, singer of hymns, etc) and into priesthoods according to which deity they served. They performed rituals, appeased the gods in order to maintain world order, and administrated the property of the temple they served. During the New Kingdom the priesthood of Ammon acquired exceptional power.

title: Temple-shaped pendant of a mummy. Gilt wood with various inlaid semi-precious stones. New Kingdom, Dynasties ΧVIII-XIX (1552-1186 BC).
The hieroglyphic symbol of Ankh.
description: Ankh was a hieroglyphic symbol and at the same time a powerful amulet protecting the living and the dead throughout the Egyptian civilization. It represents both life and breath as well as eternal life. The ankh was one of the very few hieroglyphs understood by the masses of illiterate Egyptians. Its shape, resembling a loop over a capital T, according to scholars, is either related to a primeval sexual symbol (a schematic phallus), a part of an arc or even a simple sandal strap. Probably its use began in the Pre-Dynastic Period, before 3000 B.C., as an image of a knot with some special religious-mythical significance. The main divinities are often represented holding the ankh symbol in their hands as an emblem. In many representations, in which gods hold in their hands the ankh and extend it toward the nose of the depicted living pharaoh, its connection with life-giving elements of nature– air and water – is quite perceptible. Also common are representations of the pharaoh and, later, of the common dead people being bathed by a rain of ankhs (multiple ankhs in a chain), conferring the symbolic significance of purification, regeneration, and eternal life. The ankh survives in the Coptic Period, probably because of its cross-shaped form, and passes henceforth iconographically as crux ansata (cross with a handle) with a symbolic meaning in Christianity.

In the 21th Dynasty, the offerings from the tombs of the previous pharaohs were gathered within a rocky cache in order to be protected from vandalism and plundering which was the consequence of turbulent period that followed the end of the New Kingdom. The “Royal Cache” was discovered by antiquity looters in 1880.

title: Amulet with the Egyptian symbol Djed. Lapis lazuli. Third Intermediate period (1070-712 BC).
description: The djed is an ancient Egyptian symbol for stability which features prominently in art and architecture throughout Egyptian civilization. It appeared in the Predynastic period and continued throughout the Ptolemaic. During the Old Kingdom, it was associated with god Ptah, who was given the epithet ‘’The noble Djed’’ while later on, it became one of the symbols of god Osiris.

title: Copper alloy hollow cast statue of the princess-priestess Takushit. Late period, Dynasty XXV (712-664 BC.).
description:
Lacking its base into which it was set by means of two attachments, which are rectangular in cross-section, placed on the soles of the feet. The statue was found in 1880, in Lower Egypt, on the hill of Kom-Toruga, near Lake Mariout, south of Alexandria.
It had ritual, votive and funerary functions. The statue is depicted stepping solidly on its feet with the left foot on a walking posture, indicative of movement and energy. The left arm is bent under the chest and most likely held a hieratic scepter. The right arm, extended closely against the body, held a menit or menat, a ceremonial object. The scepter and the menit affirmed her priestly status and her high social ranking since they were the symbol par excellence of priests from the upper social classes. The long, transparent clothing, which is decorated all over with incised patterns filled with precious metal wires (technique of damasking), accentuates the beautifully shaped, sensuous body. The decoration is divided into five horizontal bands, which alternate with four thinner strips at the waist, the pelvis, the thighs and the knees. 
The first band, which covers the torso, is wider. The bands are decorated with representations of divinities from the Northeastern area of the Nile Delta (the homeland of Takushit), while the strips are filled with hieroglyphs that cite prayers to these divinities. Her name means “the Ethiopian” and possibly refers to a family connection or to a marriage with an Ethiopian. 
According to the inscriptions on the statue, her father was Akan II, the Great Chief of the Libyan tribe Ma, and she was a priestess “wab” (pure-chaste priestess), which according to the religious hierarchy was the lowest priestly title. The use of the statue was ceremonial while the priestess was alive and part of the ritual equipment of the sanctuary, in which she was priestess. After her death, it was used as a votive, decorating her tomb, which, according to the custom of the time, was located within the sanctuary precinct.

title: Sistrum inscribed with the cartouche of pharaoh Amasis. Faience. Third Intermediate period. Dynasty XXVI. King Amasis (570-526 BC).
description: Temple-like sistrum (rattle). On the stem of the handle, beneath a double-face bust of goddess Hathor with ears of cow, there is an hieroglyphic inscription with the cartouche of pharaoh Amasis. The sistrum was a ceremonial musical instrument, which was handled and shaken, during cult rituals, by priestesses, women of the high social class or even by the pharaoh, when he was presenting offerings to goddess Hathor, a primeval deity with multiple roles and aspects as well as numerous cult centers. The sound of sistrum pacified the goddess and at the same time was removing and sending away the evil spirits. Hathor was regarded as mother of the pharaoh, daughter of the sun and represented his fearsome destructive eye, avenger of humankind, when the latter was acting against the law. Furthermore, she was the goddess of beauty, patroness of love, fertility, motherhood, joy, music and dance, and, finally, of the dead. Two kinds of sistrum were known in Ancient Egypt, the temple-like one, in the shape of a temple, and the arched, ring-like one, in the shape of a loop. Both kinds had a handle and were equipped with moving wires and a few bronze discs, through which the wires passed, creating sound, when shaken.

title: Solid copper alloy statue of the pharaoh Shabaka. Late period, Dynasty XXV (Nubian), (ca. 700 BC.).
description: This is the most representative portrait of Shabaka preserved in the world. A cartouche with his name is incised on his kilt’s belt. A votive statue or part of the ritual equipment of a temple from Egypt or Nubia. Since the statuette was preserved with the cartouche of the pharaoh in such good condition and the distinctive emblems of the 25th Dynasty were not lost, - like the two ureus serpents on the headdress and the necklace with heads of rams – it is one of the few attested works of the 25th Dynasty that escaped the destructive mania of the opposing Egyptian 26th Dynasty, mainly of the pharaoh Psammetichus II.

title: Statuette of an elderly official worshipping. Copper. Third Intermediate period. Dynasty XXVI.
description: Votive statue to goddess Neith. From a Sais workshop.

title: Solid copper alloy statuette formerly clad with in precious-metal leaf, representing a Nubian kneeling pharaoh making an offering to the gods. Late period, Dynasty XXVI (ca. 664-525 BC.).
description: The statuette was a votive offering, which, judging by its size, was more likely an essential piece of ritualistic equipment from a sanctuary of Egypt or Nubia. On his pleated kilt’s belt, a cartouche is incised with the name of the pharaoh Psammetichus I or II of the 26th Dynasty, known as Saite Dynasty. Nevertheless, it is likely that the cartouche refers to Psammetichus II due to the fact that he used to deform the facial characteristics of statues of previous kings and replace their cartouche with his own.

title: Canopic jar of Iahmes, priest of god Horus. Alabaster. Late period. Dynasty XXX (380-343 BC).
description:
Canopic jars were four and contained the internal organs of the body removed from the deceased’s body during mummification process. The jars were protected by the four sons of Horus which were respectively protected by goddesses. Each deity supervised one organ while each jar corresponded to a compass point. 
Baboon-headed lid: Son of Horus: Hapi. Deity: Nephthys. Point of the compass: North. Organ: lungs.

title: Funerary box of the priest Pantiamon. Wood. Late period (712-343 BC).
description: The box consists of wooden planks joined together with wooden nails and covered with white coating. Its short sides extend into a semicircle. They are designed for the protection of the ushabti. Its shape refers to the type of sanctuaries of Lower Egypt. The painted decoration of the lid bears a representation of a boat and refers to the sacred pilgrimage of the deceased to the burial place of Osiris: Abydos. It was found at the “crypt of the priests of the god Montu” in Deir Ελ-Bahari, which was discovered in 1858 by the French archaeologist Mariette. Pantiamon was probably the priest-adorner, responsible for the ritual adornment of the god’s statues.

description: Shrouds were placed over the linen wrapping of male and female mummies of the upper class in order to protect magically the deceased. Funerary amulets reinforced their magical properties.

Bronze sistrum in the shape of loop or arch. Ptolemaic period (304-30 BC).
description: The particular sistrum was a ritual rattle with four moving wires and finial in the form of goddess Isis torso. The bronze discs are missing, through which the wires passed and when shaken, they created sound. The sistrum was a ceremonial musical instrument, which was set in motion by female chanters and women of the high society, aiming to eliminate the evil powers. It was a common votive to goddess Hathor. Its sound, similar to that of the menits, recalled the sound of rustling papyri in the marshes, when crossed by Hathor in the form of a cow. Music and dance were substantial to Egyptian festivals and religious ceremonies.

title: Cat mummy. Ptolemaic period (304-30 BC.)
Copper alloy group of wrestlers. Hellenistic-Ptolemaic period. 2nd-1st c. BC. From Alexandria.
description: It symbolizes the mythic battle between Hercules and the Libyan giant Antaeus.

title: Copper alloy statuette of the god Sarapis Amun Agathodaemon. Late Hellenistic-early Roman period. First century BC-First century AD.
description: One of the rare preserved statues of this particular deity.

title: Copper alloy group of wrestlers. Hellenistic-Ptolemaic period. 2nd-1st c. BC. From Alexandria.
description: With a political and allegorical meaning. The young Ptolemy V as the divine child Horus, defeats the enemy and the forces of evil.

title: Ring with portrait of Ptolemaic queen Berenice II. Ptolemaic period. Ptolemy III Evergetes I (the Benefactor) (246-221 BC).
description: Ivory. The flat circular bezel depicts a relief portrait of queen Berenice II, the wife of Ptolemy III (246-222 B.C.). The queen is represented as goddess Isis according to the Ptolemaic tradition, wearing the fringed garment of the goddess and veil. Such rings, produced in the workshops of the Ptolemaic court, served the political propaganda of the Ptolemaic dynasty and were meant for the ladies of honor.

title: Wooden sarcophagus with the mummy of Hapi, the so-called 'Khor', son of Pami, with gilt mask. Ptolemaic period (304-150 BC).
description: It consists of separate pieces of cartonnage tied to the shroud with linen bands. It was found at Akhmim in 1884.

title: Part of papyrus sheet bearing greek script, written in black ink. Ptolemaic Period, 252 B.C. Dimensions: 0.317 x 0.135 m.
description: It was discovered in 1915 in the Fayum region of Egypt and comes from the famous archives of Zenon. Zenon, an official and administrator of the royal estate, was the assistant to the governor Apollonius, who was the head of the Ptolemaic public administration. The preserved portion is part of a letter referring to the settlement of unpaid taxes. The particular fragment was purchased, along with two more of the same group, by the Greek Ministry of Education in 1916.

title: Magic seal stone with spells and magic representation. Hellenistic-Ptolemaic period (332-30 ΒC). Semi-precious stone.
Marble statue of Alexander the Great. Roman period (30 BC-395 AD).
description: Probably part of a group erected in Alexandria in honor of Hephaestion.

title: Bronze statue of god Apis, as Roman emperor. Roman period (30 BC-395 AD).
description: Romans imposed on the Egyptians their worship as gods. In the art, Roman emperors were portrayed in the formal attire of a Pharaoh, while gods were depicted in imperial garments.

title: Male head from a mummy case. Painted limestone. Roman period. Reign of Caesar Alexander Severus (222-235 AD).
description: Part of a sarcophagus lid. The deceased’s raised head denotes his transition to immortality.

title: ‘Fayum’ funerary portrait of a man. Roman period (117-138 AD).
description: Τempera on wood.

title: ‘Fayum’ funerary portrait of a woman. Roman period (138-161 AD).
description: Encaustic painting on wood (painting technique employing a heated or cold mixture of bee wax with resin).

title: ‘Fayum’ funerary portrait of an old man. Roman period (138-161 AD).
description: Τempera on wood.

title: ‘Fayum’ funerary portrait of a young lady.  Roman period, late 4th c. AD.
description: Tempera on linen.

title: ‘Fayum’  funerary portrait of a young man. Roman period, late 4th c. AD.
description: Tempera on linen.

title: Molded glass vase for perfumes. Roman period (1st – 2nd cent. A.D.).
description: Molded glass vase for perfumes of dark blue color (cobalt blue) with high neck. It is decorated on both sides with a molded head of a youthful figure, probably Eros. The figure has a pompous face with curly hair so to speak. The vase body is created with the use of a mold while the neck is of blown glass. Perfume containers of this kind were made in the East Mediterranean, especially in Syria, and were particularly popular across the Mediterranean during the 1st and 2nd cent. A.D.

title: Crescent-shaped pendant of necklace. Gold. Roman period (138-161 AD).
description: Gold crescent-shaped pendant of a necklace, decorated with globular embossed elements in the form of seven-petal rosettes. Such pendants, considered as symbols of fertility and hanged from a chain or a gold necklace, the well-known Roman torque, were a favorite piece of jewelry for women during Roman period. The central stone in gold setting is probably a modern addition.

title: Osiris – Canopus. Roman period (2nd cent. A.D.). White marble.
description: He is depicted in the form of a handless ovoid vase with human head. The face of Osiris Canopus displays Greek features, wearing the Egyptian royal headdress, Nemes. It is one of the few preserved sculptures of this type, worldwide. At Canopus, a city in the Nile Delta, near Alexandria, the cult of Osiris-Canopus flourished around the 2nd cent. A.D. There, Osiris-Canopus, in this particular form of a vase with human head, was worshiped as a god of fertility.

title: Red Polished miniature jugs (11823, 11826, 11825)
description: Probably used to keep aromatic oils or as a child’s toy. Early Cypriot III-Middle Cypriot II period (2000-1725 BC).

title: Copper ingot in the shape of an ‘oxhide’, a type widely found throughout the Mediterranean from the 16th to the 11th c. BC . (14729)
description: The Cypriot origins of these ingots has been confirmed by lead isotope analysis.

title: Rhyton in the form of a donkey carrying Canaanite amphoras (vases of Syrian origins) on its back.  (15373)
description: It belongs to the class of plastic vessels which represent scenes of everyday life and are already known in Cyprus from the beginning of the 2nd millennium BC. Those vessels are either large clay animal figures or are rendered as plastic decorations on the rim of large vases. In Cyprus they are often found in graves as a testimony of earthly life, while in other sites of the Eastern Mediterranean they also occur in shrines. Late Cypriot III period.

title: Clay female figurine with a bird-shaped face and disproportionately large ears, from which hang two rows of hoop earrings (22654)
description: Figurines of this type copy earlier Syrian models and are predominant in the Late Cypriot II period (1450-1200 BC).

title: Phoenician jug of Bichrome Pottery,  imported to the island before the intrusion of the Phoenicians. On the belly, a strainer-spout. Cypro-Geometric ΙΙ period. 950-900 B.C.
Clay model of a chariot, with a charioteer and two warriors (17376)
description: The heads of the figures and horses were cast in a mould. It was possibly used as a toy. About 600 BC.

title: Statuette of a standing female figure holding a flower in her right hand (11974)
description: She has a tall, thin body, which is flat apart from the breast, and is undecorated at the back. She is wearing a sleeved chiton, a necklace, a polos (head cap) and ear-caps, the typical Cypriot ornament. The chiton was originally painted, as shown by some color traces. This type was commonly used to render male and female figures. In the case of female figure, it is more probable that they represented a goddess holding her symbol rather than a priestess or the woman who dedicated the statue. 550-500 BC.

title: Head of a bearded youth (1832)
description: The hair is restrained by a ribbon tied in a knot at the back. The rendering, particularly of the hair, recalls heads of kouroi from Ionia. Early 6th c. BC.

title: Figurine of enthroned Astarte on horseback. Cypro-Archaic I period (?) 750-600 B.C.
description: The goddess is wearing a high crown ''tiara'', probably decorated with flowers.  The figurine may depict a ceremony in which a procession of the statue of the enthroned goddess on horseback was taking place. This might be the reason for which the figure is rendered seated sideways.

title: Bichrome Ware IV amphora, with linear decoration and a lotus flower in black and red (29682)
description: It is one of the largest, richly decorated amphorae. Cypro-Archaic I period (750-600).

title: Headlees statuette in the type of the kore (12005)
description: She wears a long, sleeved chiton and an obliquely draped himation on which traces of red paint are preserved. Early 5th c. BC.

title: Statuette of a ‘temple servant’ (11997)
description:
The boy who is wearing a long chiton sits on the ground in the typical crouching position of the “temple servant” He probably holds a bird in his right hand and a spherical object in his left. 
Cypro-Classical II period (?). 400-310 BC.

title: Gold earrings made of twisted wire ending in a bull’s head with inlaid garnets for the eyes (1147).
description: The type possibly has its origins in Greece and became known in the Mediterranean from the 4th c. BC. 3rd c. BC.

title: White Painted lagynos, with linear decoration in a dull orange paint (11880)
description: The lagynos was the most popular wine vessel in the entire Hellenistic world.

title: Head of Herakles wearing a lion’s pelt. Marble (1833)
description: Probably from a statue in the type of the Farnese Herakles, which copies a statue of the hero carved about 325 BC by the sculptor Lysippos of Sikyon. Roman period. 30 BC-AD 330.
